newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Ex-warlord Taylor is Liberia's new president.
newsitem.headline: Ex-warlord Taylor is Liberia's new president.

text.p: Former warlord Charles Taylor won a landslide victory in Liberia's presidential election on Thursday, achieving through the ballot box what he failed to win through war.
Taylor, formally proclaimed winner of Saturday's election by the head of the election commission, told his faction rivals afterwards that he offered them a hand of friendship.
"I am not going to be a wicked president," Taylor, 49, told a news conference after the announcement of the final result triggered street celebrations by thousands of supporters.
Jubilant supporters and back-slapping former guerrillas packed his National Patriotic Party headquarters.

"To all ex-combatants... I am now your president," Taylor said. "I say to all the faction leaders, I extend my hand of friendship to you. Come on board and help in building this republic for the new millennium."
Taylor, who started the civil war in Africa's oldest republic in December 1989, won 75.3 percent of valid votes cast.
Wearing his trademark cream safari suit and smiling broadly, he was in the packed the hall at election commission headquarters to hear the news of his victory.
Former senior U.N. official Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman candidate in the field of 12, was runner-up with just under 9.6 percent. Turnout approached 90 percent.
Liberia, founded by freed American slaves in 1847, celebrates its 150th birthday on Saturday.
The elections were the climax of a peace process brokered by its West African neighbours to end a war that has killed well over 150,000 people.
Election commission chairman Henry Andrews said results of parallel polling for a 26-member Senate and a 64-seat House of Representatives would be announced in a few days.

Defeated candidates in the election commission hall congratulated Taylor but neither Johnson-Sirleaf nor Taylor's fellow former warlord Alhaji Kromah attended the ceremony. The third former warlord in the field, George Boley, was present.
Johnson-Sirleaf, Kromah and Boley alleged irregularities. None has rejected the election, declared free and fair by more than 500 international observers and over 1,000 local monitors.
Before the formal announcement of the outcome, widely expected given the pattern of previous results, Taylor extended an olive branch to his rivals.
He told BBC radio he was ready to offer jobs to some of them but he specifically mentioned Johnson-Sirleaf, 58.

"I will offer some of them senior positions and others junior positions. We must go together," Taylor said. "I intend to use the talents of most of the fellows that I have respect for, including Ellen."
Four rival candidates earlier conceded defeat.
Andrews appealed for respect for the result.
"Liberia is bigger, greater and grander than all of us," he said. "If we truly love our country...we will at this moment take a cue from the ordinary man in the street."
A Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force disarmed many of the militia fighters and ensured security during polling. Taylor has said he would like it to stay on for 12 to 18 months.
The war wrecked Liberia's iron ore, rubber, timber and diamond-based economy. It drove as many as half the pre-war population of 2.5 million people from their homes.
